pool.q: At 20 feet, the smallest letters that a child can read is the 20/60 line. You have the child walk toward the eye chart. How far does she walk before she can see the 20/20 line?
pool.rationale: 13 feet A 20/20 letter subtends a visual angle of 5 minutes of arc when viewed at 20 feet. As you move close to an object, it subtends a larger visual angle. A 20/60 letter subtends 3× the visual angle of a 20/20 letter. Using similar triangles, Therefore, the child must advance 13 feet to be 7 feet from the eye chart to see the letters (Fig. 3-6).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q1

pool.q: An adult has diplopia and a left hypertropia of 6Δ. Which combination of prisms in his glasses would help to align the two images for him? OD OS
pool.rationale: 3Δ base up 3Δbase down A strabismic deviation can be neutralized by orienting an appropriate power prism with the apex in the same direction as the deviation. A 6Δ left hypertropia can be corrected with a 6Δ base down prism in front of this eye. The prism can be divided between the eyes with 3Δ base up in front of the right eye and a 3Δ base down in front of the left (Fig. 3-7).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q2

pool.q: A 25-year-old patient with cranial nerve VI palsy is found to have an 8Δ distance esotropia. His distance prescription is plano OU. How far apart do the images of a fixation light at 6 m appear to the patient?
pool.rationale: 48 cm A prism diopter is defined as the amount of deviation of a light by the prism measured at 100 cm. For every 100 cm, light is deviated 8 cm (Fig. 3-8). At 6 m, 8Δ represents a deviation of 48 cm.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q3

pool.q: A 6Δ base-out and an 8Δ base down prism are replaced by a single prism. What is the power of this prism?
pool.rationale: 10Δ Prism power can be represented by vectors and added as this mathematical entity. The resultant vector is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs of 6 and 8, which is 10Δ base down and out at 53° (Fig. 3-9).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q4

pool.q: A +10.00 D lens is positioned as in Figure 3-1. Two laser beams are aimed parallel to the axis of the lens: one 8 mm above the axis and the other 11 mm below the axis. At what distance past the lens do the beams cross?
pool.rationale: 10 cm All rays parallel to the lens axis will converge on the secondary focal point whose location can be calculated as 100 cm/10 D = 10 cm. The result can also be obtained using Prentice’s rule and ray tracing (Fig. 3-10).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q5

pool.q: An object is located 20 cm to the left of a −2.00 D lens. Where is the image located?

options.a: 20 cm to the right of the lens
options.b: 50 cm to the right of the lens
options.c: 33 cm to the left of the lens
options.d: 14 cm to the left of the lens

pool.rationale: 14 cm to the left of the lens Vergences are indicated in Figure 3-10. Vergence of light entering the lens: A negative sign indicates diverging rays of light. Using the lens equation: The location of the resulting image can be calculated: The resulting image is 14 cm to the left of the lens.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q6

pool.q: What type and orientation does this image have?
pool.rationale: Virtual, upright Three principal rays of light can be used to locate the position and orientation of images. These rays are described here and are shown in Figure 3-11 with the convex lens: 1. A ray through the primary focal point will exit the lens parallel to the axis. 2. A ray parallel to the axis will travel through the secondary focal point. 3. A ray through the optical center of the lens will not be deviated. For the concave lens in this question, the image is virtual and upright. By ray tracing, the image can be found on the left side of the lens, thus creating a virtual image. By drawing the other principal rays, the image can be shown to be upright.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q7

pool.q: The light source and screens shown in Figure 3-2 are used to determine the power of an unknown lens. When the screen is 16 cm from the lens, a line at 45° is seen. When the screen is moved to 50 cm, the line is at 135°. What is the prescription of this lens?
pool.rationale: + 6.00 − 4.00 × 135° In the apparatus, parallel rays of light are focused by the lens onto the screen. The lens focuses light into a 45° line at 16 cm; therefore, the power of the lens in the 45° axis (and 135° meridian) is +6.00 D. Similarly, the 135° axis has a power of +2.00 D. These lines represent each end of the conoid of Sturm. The circle of least confusion falls halfway (dioptrically) between each of these lines, or at +4.00 D. This corresponds to an image on the screen at 25 cm. Figure 3-12 shows the power cross corresponding to the lens and thus the prescription: +6.00 − 4.00 × 135°.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q9

pool.q: You have two +2.00 D lenses. How far apart are the two lenses so that an object at infinity is focused 1 m to the right of the second lens?
pool.rationale: 1.5 m The best way to approach this problem is to use vergences and work from both ends toward the center. The vergence of the light entering the first lens is zero (coming from infinity). Light leaving the second lens is focused at 1 m (+1 D vergence). Using the lens equation, the vergences of light leaving the first lens and entering the second can be calculated to be +2 D and −1 D, respectively. Because they share the same intermediate image plane, the distance between the lenses is the sum of the two image distances (Fig. 3-13).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q10

pool.q: An object 25 cm from a +12.00 D lens is moved 15 cm toward the lens. How far does the image move away from the lens?
pool.rationale: 37.5 cm The amount of image movement can be calculated by measuring the difference between the image location at each position of the object (Fig. 3-14). The image moves 50.0 − 12.5 cm = 37.5 cm
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q11

pool.q: A 15-cm object is 25 cm to the left of a −2.00 D lens. How large is the resulting image?
pool.rationale: 10 cm The vergences of light entering and leaving the lens are indicated in Figure 3-15. The magnification can be calculated as a ratio of the vergence entering the lens to that leaving the lens.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q12

pool.q: Without correction, a child complains that objects closer than 33 cm are blurry. Cycloplegic refraction measured +6.00 D sphere OU. How much accommodation does this child have?
pool.rationale: 9.00 D With maximum accommodation, this child is able to focus at objects at 33 cm (3 D). Being an uncorrected hyperope, the child must accommodate through the 6.00 D of hyperopia to see clearly in the distance. An additional 3.00 D of accommodation is needed to focus at 33 cm. The total accommodation is 9.00 D.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q13

pool.q: What reading add is needed to his corrected distance prescription so that at 40 cm this patient uses half of his accommodative amplitude?
pool.rationale: No reading add needed The far point and near points correspond to + 5.00 D and plano; thus, the patient has 5 D of accommodation. With a +5.00 D distance prescription, he has the required 2.50 D of accommodation to focus at 40 cm (Fig. 3-16).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q15

pool.q: When looking at an object at 25 cm, a patient has an esotropia of 30Δ. With +3.00 D glasses, his esotropia decreases to 15Δ. What is his distance esodeviation without glasses?
pool.rationale: 10Δ Using the gradient method for calculating the accommodative convergence/accommodation ratio: For every diopter of accommodation, the patient increases his esotropia by 5Δ. At a distance, he accommodates 4 D less than at 25 cm; therefore, his uncorrected distance deviation will be 30 − (4 × 5) = 10Δ.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q16

pool.q: A Galilean telescope is constructed with a +5.00 D objective and a −10.00 D eyepiece. What is the magnification of this telescope?
pool.rationale: 2× A Galilean telescope is constructed with converging and diverging lenses such that the primary focal point of the objective lens corresponds to the secondary focal point of the eyepiece lens. As a result, parallel rays from infinity entering the objective emerge as parallel rays from the eyepiece. Angular magnification occurs, which corresponds to the ratio of the power of the eyepiece to the power of the objective.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q17

pool.q: You have a +10 D lens and a +20 D lens. You want to make a 2× magnifier. What is the distance between the lenses to produce this magnification?
pool.rationale: 15 cm An astronomical telescope is constructed of two convex (plus) lenses (Fig. 3-17). The secondary focal point of the first lens (objective) corresponds to the primary focal point of the second lens (eyepiece). The corresponding focal points of each lens in this case are 10 and 5 cm for a total of 15 cm. Incidentally, the astronomical telescope forms an inverted image.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q18

pool.q: How much accommodation is required to view an object 1 m in front of the +10 D lens?
pool.rationale: 5 D The vergences can be calculated in Figure 3-18. Plastic Glass
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q19

pool.q: A 10Δ plastic prism and a 10Δ crown glass prism are placed under water. Under water, how much do the plastic and glass prisms deviate light? Plastic Glass
pool.rationale: <10Δ <10Δ Consider the situation when one surface of the prism is perpendicular to the beam of light (Prentice’s position) as shown in Figure 3-19. The refraction of light only occurs at the second surface. The refraction at this interface obeys Snell’s Law: nplastic sin θ1 = nwater sin θ2. Because nplastic > nwater, less bending of light will occur at the plastic–water interface than the plastic–air interface, effectively reducing the prismatic power of the lens. A glass lens will have a similar decrease in prismatic power.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q20

pool.q: Prescription swimming goggles are constructed from plastic (n = 1.45) planoconcave lenses. They measure −2.00 D in air. What is the power of the goggles when worn underwater (n = water 1.33)?
pool.rationale: −2.00 D When worn properly, the goggles (Fig. 3-20) have a plano surface at the water–plastic interface and thus no deviation of light. The power of the prescription is ground into the plastic–air interface. Underwater, this compartment should still contain air; therefore, no change in prescription power results. Appears Appears Closest Appears Midway Farthest
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q21

pool.q: An aquarium is 25 cm deep. A rock is viewed from above the aquarium. The water (n = 1.33) is then removed and replaced with silicone oil (n = 1.40). How does the location of the rock appear when viewed through the air, water, and oil? Appears Closest Appears Midway Appears Farthest
pool.rationale: Oil Water Air Consider the three scenarios: 1. Air (n = 1.00) No refraction occurs. 2. Water (n = 1.33) Refraction occurs at air–water interface. The stone appears closer than it actually is. 3. Oil (n = 1.40) Higher index of refraction increases degree of bending of light, making the stone seem even closer (Fig. 3-21).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q22

pool.q: A pair of −10.0 D glasses were supposed to be made from high-index plastic (n = 1.67), but instead, a lens with identical thickness and curvature was made from a different material. What can be said about this new lens?

options.a: The new lens will also measure −10.0 D since the lens thickness and curvature are identical.
options.b: If the new lens was made from a material with n = 1.74, the lens will measure weaker than 10.0 D.
options.c: If the new lens measured −8.80 D, the material could be polycarbonate (n = 1.59).

pool.rationale: If the new lens measured −8.80 D, the material could be polycarbonate (n = 1.59). If two lenses are identical except for a difference in refractive index (Table 3-1), the lens with the higher refractive index will result in a greater amount of light refraction (Snell’s law). Thus, the lens with the n = 1.74 would result in a prescription stronger than −10.0 D. Material Index of Refraction CR39 1.49 Trivex 1.53 Polycarbonate 1.59 High-index plastic 1.6–1.76 Crown glass 1.525
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q23

pool.q: A phakic patient undergoes a vitrectomy with replacement of his vitreous fluid (n = 1.34) with silicone oil (n = 1.40). What change occurs in his prescription?

options.d: Cannot be determined with the information given

pool.rationale: Myopic shift Silicone oil has a higher index of refraction than vitreous, so more refraction occurs at the posterior lens interface. This is similar to having a lens with a much higher dioptric power within the eye. The resultant prescription for the eye becomes more myopic.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q25

pool.q: An object is 100 cm from a +4 D concave mirror. What type and orientation of image is formed?
pool.rationale: Real, inverted
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q26

pool.q: Where is the image located?

options.a: 20 cm to the right of the mirror
options.b: 20 cm to the left of the mirror
options.c: 33 cm to the right of the mirror
options.d: 33 cm to the left of the mirror

pool.rationale: 33 cm to the left of the mirror Using the vergence formula: U + D = V −1 + 4 = + 3 Because V is positive, a real image located on the same side of the mirror as the object is formed. Because U and V have opposite signs, the image is inverted compared to the object. The location of the image is 1/V = 1/3 m = 0.33 m to the left of the mirror (Fig. 3-22). Ray tracing and vergence calculations also allow determination of the answer to these questions. Remember that mirrors flip object and image space. Therefore, the plus vergence “leaving” the mirror actually converges toward the left.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q27

pool.q: An object is 12.5 cm from a +3 D lens that is 10 cm from a plane mirror. How far apart are the image and object?
pool.rationale: 187.5 cm This problem can be separated into each optical component, and they can be considered independently from each other. The first lens (Fig. 3-23) produces a virtual image (Img ) 20 cm to the left of the lens (and 30 cm to the left of the mirror). This image becomes the object (Obj ) of the mirror (Fig. 3-24). The image (Img ) of the mirror becomes the object (Obj ) of the lens again (Fig. 3-25). Note 2 3 that the light is now traveling from right to left because object space is to the right of the lens. The final image (Img ) is 200 cm to the left of the lens and 187.5 cm from the initial object.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q28

pool.q: You use the duochrome test to refine the refraction of a patient. The patient says the red letters are much clearer than the green letters. The patient is:
pool.rationale: Overplussed The duochrome test relies on the differential degree of refraction experienced by shorter and longer wavelengths of light. Shorter wavelengths (violet, blue, green) are bent more than longer wavelengths (orange, red) (Fig. 3-26). The difference in refraction between red and green is approximately 0.50 D. In this case, the red portion of the spectrum is focused sharply on the retina. The endpoint of the duochrome test is to straddle the spectrum on the retina with red wavelengths posterior and green wavelengths anterior. This can be accomplished by adding diverging lenses (or removing converging lenses) to move the spectrum more posteriorly. The patient is therefore overplussed.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q29

pool.q: You see the following reflex (Fig. 3-3) when performing streak retinoscopy on a patient. What needs to be done to neutralize this reflex?

options.a: Rotate axis 15° clockwise, add positive sphere
options.b: Rotate axis 15° counterclockwise, add negative sphere
options.c: Rotate axis 15° counterclockwise, add positive sphere
options.d: Rotate axis 15° clockwise, add negative sphere

pool.rationale: Rotate axis 15° clockwise, add negative sphere Among the phenomena seen with streak retinoscopy, the break phenomenon is demonstrated here. It occurs when the streak and reflex are off axis. The streak should be rotated 15° clockwise so that it is parallel to the reflex. As neutrality is approached, the reflex becomes wider until it fills the whole pupil. In this case of against movement, negative sphere is needed to neutralize the reflex.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q30

pool.q: You hold a +1.00 D lens in front of a patient. At a working distance of 67 cm, you see against motion with the streak oriented at 90° and less against movement with the streak oriented at 180°. Which situation exists for this patient?
pool.rationale: Compound myopic astigmatism Against motion requires minus lenses to neutralize the reflex. The myopia is greater in the 180° meridian, which is measured with the streak oriented at 90°. The working distance of 67 cm corresponds to 1.50 D that needs to be subtracted from the lens in front of the eye. The +1.00 D lens only partially compensates for the working distance. Removing this lens still leaves the prescription myopic.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q31

pool.q: You perform streak retinoscopy on a cyclopleged infant. With the streak oriented vertically at 90°, you neutralize the reflex with a −2.00 D lens (after subtracting the working distance), and with the horizontal streak, +3.00 D lens. What is the cycloplegic refraction?
pool.rationale: −2.00 + 5.00 × 180° With the streak oriented vertically and by moving it left and right, the power in the 180° meridian (and the power in the 90° axis) is actually being evaluated—likewise, when the beam is rotated 90°. This evaluation can be represented on the power cross in Figure 3-27. The astigmatism is the difference between the two lenses, or +5.00 D. The final prescription is −2.00 + 5.00 × 180°.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q32

pool.q: A patient wears +3.00 + 2.25 × 60°. If all of her astigmatism is corneal, what could her keratometry measure?
pool.rationale: 41.25 D at 150°, 43.50 D at 60° The power cross for the patient’s prescription is drawn in Figure 3-28. Remember that the power of the cylinder is 90° from its axis. The 2.25 D of astigmatic power of the glasses is oriented in the 150° meridian to correspond to the cornea’s steeper meridian. The only K reading that is oriented properly with the correct amount of astigmatism is 41.25 D at 150°, 43.50 D at 60°.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q33

pool.q: An uncorrected, cyclopleged patient looks at an Amsler grid 40 cm away. The vertical lines are focused sharply when a +4.75 D sphere is held in front of this eye. The horizontal lines are sharpest with a +6.00 D sphere. What is her distance correction?
pool.rationale: +2.25 + 1.25 × 180° When looking at an object at 40 cm, 2.5 D of accommodation is needed. The distance lenses would be +2.25 D and +3.50 D, respectively. The power of a lens in the horizontal meridian is responsible for focusing the vertical lines. This corresponds to the +3.50 D cylinder with axis at 90°. The cylinder power with axis 180° is +2.25 D.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q34

pool.q: A patient wears the following prescription: −1.00 + 2.00 × 180° Add +3.00 OU −2.50 + 1.00 × 90° His bifocal segment is located 10 mm inferior to the optical center of the glasses. How much relative prism is induced when he looks through the top of his bifocal?
pool.rationale: 3.50Δ right base up The power crosses pictured in Figure 3-29 correspond to the lenses in his glasses. The prisms induced by the bifocals are equal in each eye and cancel each other. When one looks downward, only the power in the 90° meridian is deviating light. Prentice’s rule is used to calculate the prismatic effect of the lenses: OD: (+1.00 D) × (1.0 cm) = 1.00Δ Base up OS: (−2.50 D) × (1.0 cm) = 2.50Δ Base down Combining the prisms results in 3.50Δ base up over the right eye.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q35

pool.q: An aphakic patient wears +10.00 D glasses at a vertex distance of 10 mm. What power of contact lens should be ordered to fit on K’s?
pool.rationale: +11.0 D The far point of the eye is located 10 cm behind the spectacle plane (9 cm behind the cornea) (Fig. 3-30). A lens placed on the cornea would need a power of 100/9 cm = +11.1 D to focus light at this same point. The lens effectivity formula may also be used to determine the same result: Where D1 and D2 are the old and new lens powers (diopters), respectively, and s is the distance the lens is moved (meters) toward the eye.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q36

pool.q: A patient has K’s of 42.00 D at 90°/40.00 D at 180° and refraction of −1.50 + 0.50 × 90°. A plano hard contact lens is fit on the flatter K. What overrefraction is measured?
pool.rationale: −1.00 + 1.50 × 180° The cornea is steeper along the 90° meridian as pictured in Figure 3-31 (with-the-rule astigmatism). A contact lens fit on the flatter K would create a concave tear lens with 2 D of power along the 90° meridian. Looking at the power crosses for the tear lens and overrefraction, the answer can be calculated to be −1.00 + 1.50 × 180° (Fig. 3-32).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q37

pool.q: Which change would allow a hard contact lens to fit more tightly to a cornea?

options.a: Decreasing the diameter from 8.80 mm to 8.40 mm
options.b: Decreasing the base curve from 8.20 mm to 8.00 mm
options.c: Increasing the optical zone from 8.20 mm to 8.40 mm
options.d: Increasing the power from −3.00 D to −3.50 D

pool.rationale: Decreasing the base curve from 8.20 mm to 8.00 mm Decreasing the base curve makes the lens steeper and thus causes a tighter fit. Decreasing the lens diameter increases the mobility of the lens and thus causes a looser fit. The size of the optical zone and power of the lens do not affect the fit of a lens (Fig. 3-33).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q38

pool.q: Which one of the following single changes results in the selection of a lens more powerful than intended?

options.a: Using an A-constant of 116.8 instead of 117.3
options.b: Axial length measured as 20.5 mm rather than 20.2 mm
options.c: Average keratometry of 44.50 D in place of 44.00 D
options.d: Placing the lens in the ciliary sulcus instead of in the capsular bag

pool.rationale: Placing the lens in the ciliary sulcus instead of in the capsular bag The lens power formula is dependent on axial length (in millimeters) and keratometry (in diopters) as follows: Lens power = A − 2.5 (axial length) − 0.9 (average keratometry) A higher A-constant, decreased axial length, or decreased keratometry readings would result in the calculation of a stronger lens. Moving a convex (plus) lens more anteriorly in the eye and away from the nodal point also effectively increases its power.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q39

pool.q: A diffractive multifocal IOL is designed with concentric rings of differing power to provide a 2.5 D range of focus. The lens was implanted and the patient complains that he is unable to read at all at near, but distance is fine. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this?

options.b: Lens power is too weak and patient is hyperopic at distance.
options.d: The lens is not moving within the eye enough to provide the near focus.

pool.rationale: Lens power too weak and patient is hyperopic at distance A diffractive multifocal lens is typically designed with alternating zones of far and near (Fig. 34A). This produces a defocus curve with two peaks corresponding to the focal points for distance and near (Fig. 34B). When there is a residual prescription, the defocus curve is shifted. In particular, when the lens power is not strong enough (and the patient would measure hyperopic at distance), the curve is shifted left. This patient is seeing distance with the near peak of the curve. Mild astigmatism would affect vision at all distances. Decentration of the lens could cause more side effects such as haloes and glare, but would not be expected to affect acuity to such a large extent. Finally, the diffractive multifocal is not designed to move within the eye like an accommodative IOL.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q40

pool.q: A patient is having cataract surgery with a toric IOL in her right eye. We have the following measurements: K’s 42.5 @ 45°/44.0 @ 135° Refraction: −3.00 + 1.50 × 60° with acuity of 20/80 AL: 22.79 mm Incision location: 8 o’clock What axis is the best orientation for this IOL?
pool.rationale: 135° The toric IOL is typically oriented on the steep axis of the corneal astigmatism. Minor adjustments of axis may be needed to account for incision location and presence of limbal relaxing incisions. The degree and orientation of astigmatism as measured in the refraction can be incorrect as the cataract may be inducing astigmatism in addition to the cornea.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q41

pool.q: A patient had a −10 D myopic LASIK treatment years ago. Now, she presents for cataract surgery. Which change introduces the most error in the lens calculations compared to her eye if it had never had LASIK?
pool.rationale: Corneal curvature measurements LASIK achieves a change in the prescription by the microscopic removal of corneal tissue and reshaping the anterior contour of the cornea. The amount of tissue removed is in the order of 100 µm (0.01 mm). The amount of change in axial length is small compared to the changes in keratometry. Depending on the location of corneal curvature measured, there can be large variations in values, with the central cornea being much flatter. This introduces the most error in the lens calculations.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q42

pool.q: A patient had a −10 D myopic LASIK treatment years ago. Now, she presents for cataract surgery. All of the following measurements would be helpful in the calculation of the lens power for cataract surgery in this patient except:
pool.rationale: Central corneal thickness A number of formulas have been developed to calculate the IOL power after LASIK and refractive surgery, including the Aramberri Double K method, clinical history method, Masket method, and others. These rely upon pre-and postoperative refractions and keratometry, the LASIK treatment, and adjustments to these measurements. Although corneal thickness may influence the curvature of the cornea, the actual corneal curvature measurements and refractions are the most useful in the calculations for lens power post-LASIK.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q43

pool.q: What strength of lens is needed so that a patient with 20/160 visual acuity can read newsprint without accommodation?
pool.rationale: +8.00 D Kestenbaum’s rule dictates the power of a lens needed to allow a patient with low vision to read newsprint. The power of lens is equal to the reciprocal of the visual acuity, that is, 160/20 = 8 D.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q44

pool.q: Which optical principle is the basis for antireflective coatings on glasses and lenses?
pool.rationale: Interference Antireflective coatings are based on interference of light to eliminate the reflection of certain wavelengths (Fig. 3-35). Thin coatings of plastic are placed on the surface of a lens such that certain wavelengths are reflected and are one-half wavelength out of phase with light reflected at the first interface. The destructive interference effectively negates these waveforms. Diffraction is the bending of light rays when they pass through a thin grating or pinhole. Polarization is the elimination of light energy not vibrating along a particular axis. Coherence is a measure of the degree of the uniformity of a wavelength.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q45

pool.q: A polarized lens is oriented so that it eliminates the vertical component of white light. Light polarized at 45° is projected through the lens. What percentage of the light is transmitted through the lens?
pool.rationale: 71% Using a vector to represent the light (Fig. 3-36), a polarizing filter can eliminate the vertical vector component. The light intensity corresponds to the magnitude of the vector. Thus, 71% of the light is transmitted through the lens. This may seem counterintuitive, but vectors do not add algebraically (unless they are both oriented in the same direction). Polarizing filters that are oriented perpendicular to each other do not let any light through.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q46

pool.q: A patient purchased a pair of sunglasses with a dark blue tint. Which of these colors would be the hardest to see?
pool.rationale: Blue A blue lens would block to the greatest extent the blue wavelengths of light and permit transmission of the other wavelengths. This property is utilized in fundus photography where blue light is projected into the eye. A filter in the camera blocks the reflected blue wavelengths but permits the fluorescent green light to be transmitted and recorded on film.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q47

pool.q: Looking through the inferior prism of a Zeiss 4-mirror goniolens, you see the following in the slit lamp (Fig. 3-4): Where is the foreign body located in the trabecular meshwork?
pool.rationale: 11 o’clock The Zeiss goniolens allows a view of the angle by using a mirror to direct light obliquely across the cornea (Fig. 3-37). The mirror in this view reverses superior and inferior but not left and right. Looking through the interior gonioprism, the superior angle is visualized. The foreign body corresponds to the 11 o’clock position.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q48

pool.q: Which optical instrument provides an inverted and reversed image of the retina?

options.c: Hruby lens and slit lamp (10× objective magnification)
options.d: Goldmann contact lens and slit lamp (10× objective magnification)

pool.rationale: Indirect ophthalmoscope with 20 D lens Ophthalmic instruments use a combination of external lenses (Table 3-2) and the cornea/lens system to create an image of the retina. Less magnification permits a larger field of view whereas greater magnification results in less depth of focus but higher resolution of details. The appropriate ophthalmic instrument permits the viewing of different aspects of the retina. pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q49

pool.q: A patient has a red Maddox rod with the cylinders oriented horizontally placed over her left eye. What does she see when she views a distant white fixation light?
pool.rationale: White light, vertical red line Maddox rods are cylinders of high plus power (Fig. 3-38). Light is focused very close to the rods (too close to actually see); instead, a virtual image perpendicular to these lights is visible. The left eye sees a vertical red line produced by the Maddox rod. The right eye sees a single white light.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Optics, Q50
